“Bat defence,” © Daniel Meier / CUPOTY “This moth is in an evolutionary arms race against bats – sonar versus expert stealth. Bats are fierce nigh-time aerial predators with impressive sonar for targeting flying moths. This moth, (Eucyclodes fascinans) has evolved advanced stealth to try and evade detection. Those wild tufts coming off the thorax aren’t just for show, they play a crucial role in anti-air defence, helping protect the moth’s most vital parts (the tastiest bits) from bats. The tufts interfere with bat echolocation by breaking up and absorbing sound, making the moth harder to detect.”
There’s a lot of wonder to see in the world if you just look closely. One photo contest celebrates the smaller things in nature you might miss at first glance. Called Close-up Photographer of the Year (CUPOTY), the competition recognizes close-up, macro, and micro photography from creatives worldwide. The eighth (2026) edition of CUPOTY has just announced its shortlist, narrowing the top 100 photos from a record 15,388 entries.
“Close-up photography has a wonderful way of revealing details and perspectives that often go unnoticed,” says competition co-founder Tracy Calder. “This year’s shortlist is a fabulous showcase of imagination, technical expertise, and natural curiosity.” The shortlist spans 11 galleries and covers everything from animals, arachnids, and insects to intimate landscapes, studio art, and underwater scenes.
The selected images showcase amazing details that highlight the unique—and often life-saving—characteristics of varying creatures. In Bat Defense , photographer Daniel Meier captured a portrait of a moth that has evolved to evade detection by bats, a fierce aerial predator. The image highlights the long, wild hairs on either side of the moth’s large eyes, which help keep it safe from bats; the hair tufts break up and absorb sound, making it harder for bats to detect the moth through echolocation.
While Meier looks to insects, Lukas Furlan shows us would-be openings to another world. In Untitled 14 , the photographer shot a mind-bending image in which a landscape is reflected in a puddle. Rocks and dust surround the reflection, making it look as if Furlan stumbled upon a gateway. “I was already fascinated by this scene,” he writes, “but rotating the image later revealed an entirely different world, almost like looking through a portal. It’s a reminder of the magic of experimentation and unexpected discoveries in photography.”

A piano player is giving back joy to the place that gave her back health.
“I came here as a patient, and now I can give something back,” said 84-year-old Bonnie Fay, who first came to Bryn Mawr Village nursing home in Pennsylvania.
Guillain-Barré syndrome, a rare disorder in which the body’s immune system attacks its own nerves, had left her paralyzed, and she arrived at the nursing facility facing a long and uncertain recovery.
In those difficult weeks, she found comfort in the one thing that had been with her since childhood.
“I found that the piano was very good for me,” Fay said. “It lifted my spirits tremendously.”
Somewhere along the way, GNN was told, she made herself a promise. She thought, ‘someday I’ll come back and play here.'”
Today, and despite her advanced years, Fay fulfills that promise regularly, playing the Bryn Mawr Village piano for residents recovering from illness, surgery, and injury. She had been a patient here not once, but twice—the first time after a series of about 7 orthopedic surgeries.
“Bryn Mawr Village helped me through some very hard times, and I never forgot that,” Fay said. “When I wanted to come back and play, they arranged to pick me up and bring me here. That meant a great deal to me.”
Born in Philadelphia, she grew up in South Jersey and Penn Valley and began studying piano at age 7.

items.title: A Rare Surviving Letter From Martha Washington Sheds Light on Her Young Daughter's Struggle With Epilepsy
items.desc: Recently obtained by the Library of Congress, the 1760 letter offers positive news about the health of four-year-old Martha Parke Custis, known as Patsy, the stepdaughter of George Washington
items.text:
More than 260 years ago, Martha Washington wrote to a friend with encouraging news about her young daughter’s health. Now, that letter has found a new home at the Library of Congress, offering a rare glimpse into the family’s private life.
Martha penned the note on September 29, 1760. Writing to Margaret Bolan Green, she provided an update on her four-year-old daughter “Patsy.”
“I have the pleasure to tell you my dear little girl is much better,” she wrote. “She has lost her fitts & fevours bout and seems to be getting well very fast.”
The Library of Congress purchased the letter for $47,500 in June during a Heritage Auctions sale, with funding from the James Madison Council’s Edwin L. Cox Legacy Trust, a permanent endowment that helps the library acquire materials. The library already had 11 of Martha’s letters, but this is the first that bears her handwriting.
“Very few of Martha Washington’s letters survive, as she appears to have destroyed most of her own private correspondence,” Elizabeth Novara , the American women’s history specialist for the library’s Manuscript Division, writes in a blog post . “Even brief documentation of her relationships with family and friends, as may be found in this letter, is important to understanding women’s lives during this time period.”
“Patsy”—whose full name was Martha Parke Custis —was one of the four children Martha had with her first husband, Daniel Parke Custis . The two had been married for just seven years when Custis died from a sudden illness in July 1757, at the age of 45. Two years later, at age 27, the widowed Martha married George Washington. Together, they raised the two surviving children from Martha’s first marriage, Patsy and John “Jacky” Parke Custis . (The other two, Daniel Parke Custis and Frances Parke Custis, died while their father was still alive.).
Historians believe that William Costin , a prominent member of Washington, D.C.’s free Black community, was likely Martha Washington’s grandson —the child of her son from her first marriage, Jacky, and an enslaved woman.
Martha wrote the letter after George Washington had served as commander of the Virginia Regiment during the French and Indian War but before he had become the nation’s first president . Historians now suspect that Patsy’s “fitts & fevours” were symptoms of epilepsy , a neurological disorder caused by abnormal bursts of electrical activity in the brain. But, at the time, doctors didn’t understand her affliction.

A man who received nothing but hate mail for his Halloween hobby proved to be just the treat that Tammy Wyche needed to brighten her weekly drive to cancer treatment appointments.
Though a front yard covered in skeletons might serve to remind someone of their mortality, Wyche marveled at the creativity with which the homeowner arranged his decorations.
Some were raising the flag at Iwo Jima, while another was giving its dog a bone. There was a bony beekeeper who stood behind a cowboy riding an osseous equine, not far from where two boneheaded tourists were taking a selfie.
Yet despite this macabre menagerie, the scariest thing to Mr. Bill Pyle was what tended to show up in his Oxford, Ohio mailbox in those weeks leading up to Halloween—accusations of devil worship, promises of his expedient arrival in hell, and other such condemnations.
This carried on year after year, until one fateful day when Pyle opened a letter that he said stopped him “dead in his tracks.”
“I have been driving past your house daily for the past 19 days on my way to radiation treatments. A highlight of my journey has been checking to see who else has joined the bone family & what they are up to,” Wyche wrote in a heartfelt, handwritten correspondence.
“Thankfully, Wed. Sept 11th is my final radiation treatment, though I may need to continue to drive by once in a while to see what’s new. Thanks for the diversion.”
“Tears came to my eyes,” Pyle told CBS News’ ‘On the Road’ with Steve Hartman, remembering when he read it the first time. “[It]really touched my heart.”
Seeing the date of her final treatment, Pyle decided to roll the bones on a big surprise for this special admirer.
When Wyche drove past the ‘Bone Family’ that Wednesday morning, she looked to the right and saw a whole skeleton crew cheering her on with signs that celebrated this final milestone.
“It was very touching to think that somebody would go to that effort for a stranger,” she said.
Thanks to the story of Wyche’s brush with death at Pyle’s house, for every one person that has a bone to pick with him, there are 30—from as far away as Australia—sending messages of appreciation that encourage him to keep going with his skeletons.

items.text:
Watching adults misunderstand the cues of his autistic cousin, a teen taught himself machine learning to build technology that could help them.
His solution has more than 700 users in 12 countries, reaching families through autism therapy centers—all while remaining free.
Kora, a free app that helps parents and caregivers read the emotional cues of autistic children. The app will offer several possible readings of what an autistic child may be feeling without any scores, diagnoses, or judgements.
The story begins with the younger cousin of New Jersey high schooler Shashank Madala, who would on occasion get upset at family gatherings. The adults who loved him most would gather around and guess out loud about whether he was hungry or whether the room was too loud.
They were often wrong, Madala writes, and over time the boy stopped trying to tell them. Madala was just 15, with a single computer science class behind him, but nevertheless decided to take action.
Madala’s early versions of Kora gave caregivers one fast, confident answer, and he came to see that this repeated the very mistake his family had made with his cousin. He rebuilt the app to slow adults down, offering more than one possible reading and surfacing what it is least sure about.
The philosophy behind his work was that technology aimed at autistic children is often built to change the child. His aim was to flip that script.
“A tool that announces that a child is angry invites the adult to stop looking at the child,” he wrote in Autism Spectrum News in August.
A caregiver points a phone camera at the child, and Kora offers several possible readings of what the child may be feeling, with bars for happy, sad, angry, afraid, and neutral, along with suggestions for how to respond.
In a display of responsible use of AI beyond his years, Madala also programmed Kora to now flag when it is unsure, leaving the final judgment to the adult who knows the child.

items.text:
Combining body mass index with other measurements and tests would lead to better care and outcomes, experts say
An alternative to BMI for diagnosing obesity could prevent misdiagnosis in millions of people worldwide, according to doctors who found it more accurately distinguished healthy people from those with harmful excess body fat.
Medical experts have long considered body mass index a blunt instrument for defining obesity, leading to concerns that substantial numbers of people with excess body fat are missed while others who are healthy are wrongly diagnosed.
The new approach, which combines BMI with other body measurements and organ function tests, suggests BMI alone misses obesity in 5-9% of adults, while wrongly diagnosing the condition in as many as 3%.
“This misclassification can account for tens of millions of people, so the inaccuracy of BMI is a big problem at scale and also for individuals,” said Francisco Rubino, a professor of metabolic and bariatric surgery at King’s College London.
BMI is calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by height in metres squared. About 1.6 billion people worldwide are classified as overweight, meaning their BMI falls between 25 and 29.9, and nearly a billion with a BMI of 30 or more are considered obese. Two-thirds of adults in the UK and more than 70% of adults in the US are overweight or obese based on BMI alone.
Rubino and his colleagues drew on health records from more than 800,000 people in the UK, US, China and Spain to test a diagnostic approach for obesity that he and other world experts proposed last year in a Lancet Commission report . They used the records to track people’s health for up to 15 years.
Under the new definition, someone with a BMI over 40 is considered obese, but doctors check people with a lower BMI for excess body fat by looking at their waist measurement.
A BMI of 30-plus with a raised waist measurement or waist-to-height ratio counts as obese, as does a BMI from 25 to 29.9 if waist measurement and waist-to-height ratio are high. In most countries, a raised waist measurement means more than 102cm (40in) for men and 88cm for women, while thresholds for a high waist-to-height ratio are about 0.57.
In a second step of the diagnosis, doctors distinguish between clinical obesity, meaning an active disease where excess body fat is already impairing organ function, and pre-clinical obesity, where the extra fat is a health risk but has yet to cause problems.

items.title: Global Fossil Fuel Emissions Are Expected to Drop This Year, Partly Because of the Conflicts in Iran and Ukraine
items.desc: The small decrease seems to stem partially from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a major global chokepoint for oil transportation. Scientists say that the decline will not last without the accelerated deployment of renewable energies
items.text:
In 2020, humans hunkered down amid the Covid-19 pandemic, contributing to an unprecedented 7 percent decrease in global fossil fuel emissions , according to the Global Carbon Project, an international collaboration that releases annual reports on emissions trends. For the first time since then, emissions are expected to fall again, although to a lesser degree.
Global Carbon Project researchers predict that in 2026, countries will have emitted 42.1 billion U.S. tons of planet-warming carbon dioxide, a 0.4 percent decrease compared with the previous year. That’s partly because of growing solar and wind power, but also a surge in oil prices and supply chain issues sparked by the United States-Israel war with Iran.
The team described these findings in a preprint report, which has not been peer-reviewed, released on November 10 in the journal Earth System Data Science . Some of the scientists also published an analysis in the journal Nature Climate Change .
“A decline in fossil [carbon dioxide] emissions is encouraging, but a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution,” says report and study co-author Pierre Friedlingstein , a climate scientist at the University of Exeter in England, in a statement . “The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies. While renewables and electric vehicles are increasingly offsetting growth in energy demand, further acceleration is needed if global emissions are to peak and enter a sustained decline.”
According to Friedlingstein and colleagues’ calculations, emissions from oil and gas are projected to decline this year by 1.9 and 0.3 percent, respectively. However, that’s partially offset by a 0.6 percent rise in emissions from coal. (Burning coal generates more pollution than oil or gas.)
In 2020, levels of methane—the second-largest contributor to climate change—surprisingly spiked. Earlier this year, researchers reported that the unexpected surge was caused by dynamics in the atmosphere and natural sources of the gas, including wetlands.
China emits around one-third of the world’s fossil emissions, making it the country that produces the most carbon dioxide. This year, its emissions declined overall, despite a small bump in coal pollution. That’s likely because China is leading the clean energy transition—it’s responsible for half of global emissions avoided due to renewable energy and electric vehicles.

items.title: Campaigners want more land protected from housing
items.desc: After parkland was safeguarded from development, residents want the council to change a housing plan.
items.text:
Residents in King's Lynn are campaigning for more green space to be protected
After a successful campaign getting parkland protected, residents in a Norfolk town are asking for more space to be given the same safeguards from development.
Seven acres (2.8 hectares) of land known as Harding's Pits, beside the River Great Ouse in King's Lynn, will be preserved after it was given "village green status" by the county council .
The Harding's Pits Community Association had campaigned for the past 30 years to keep the area as leisure space.
Next, the group wants the protection to be extended to the east side, which has been earmarked for up to 50 houses in King's Lynn and West Norfolk Borough Council's local plan , external . The authority has been approached for comment.
The land in the foreground has been given protected status, but the space closer to the town centre at the top has been earmarked for housing
Alexandra Kemp, an independent councillor, said she was asking her authority to amend its local plan.
She said: "I want to protect the east side of Hardings Way as a village green. To take out the 50 houses earmarked for Harding's Pits east from the borough's local plan, and provide community sports facilities, more trees and places for wildlife instead.
"Any development along Hardings Way risks more general traffic which would be devastating to the peace, quiet, safety, and amenity and wildlife."
The local council has been given a target to build more than 10,000 new homes by 2040 by the government.
Harding's Pits is located alongside the River Great Ouse
Harding's Pits was turned into a public space in the early 1960s, but was originally a 19th Century clay pit which was then used as landfill.
The site is currently used for dog walking and as pedestrian access to King's Lynn town centre.

items.text:
Sculptures of bears and bees will be displayed across Jersey
A new public art trail will mark the arrival of Asiatic black bears, Jersey Zoo has said.
Sculptures of bears and bees would be put up across the island's wild landscapes, coastal spots and urban spaces to celebrate the arrival of the new species in their new enclosure next year, said bosses.
They said the installation, which launches in July next year, aimed to shine a light on "connections that sustain the natural world, from its largest inhabitants to its smallest".
Artists will be invited to submit designs to turn the sculptures into "distinctive works of art" while schools and community groups will also be encouraged to participate.
It is hoped the sculptures will then be sold a fundraising auction at the end of the summer.
Rebecca Brewer, chief executive of Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust, said: "We want everyone who connects with our work, whether at Jersey Zoo or through our conservation projects around the world, to feel they can make a difference for nature.
"Our public art trails are a wonderful way to bring that belief to life."

items.title: The swan sanctuary wetland fighting climate change
items.desc: The global campaign to restore the "soggy secret weapon" that can combat against climate change.
items.text:
Swans and ducks have enjoyed the wetland reserve at Slimbridge for 80 years
Most people know rainforests are vital in the fight against climate change, but now scientists say wetlands could be even more important.
Saltmarshes, mangrove swamps and wetlands can absorb carbon "four times faster than trees", according to the charity the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT).
Celebrating 80 years since WWT's first wetland bird reserve was founded at Slimbridge, in Gloucestershire, the charity's leaders have called for one million hectares of wetlands to be restored across the world.
Sarah Fowler, CEO of WWT, said: "They are mood-boosting, flood-buffering, water-purifying, incredible habitats. But we have lost 85% of the world's wetlands."
Sir Peter Scott feeds migrating swans and geese at Slimbridge in 1947, with Desmond Hawkins, BBC features producer from Bristol
WWT now runs 10 wetland bird reserves across the UK.
Many people come to enjoy the swans, geese, flamingoes and migrating wildfowl, but do not realise how powerful these habitats can be in soaking up carbon and slowing down climate change.
So how vital are wetlands for birds, and how powerful can they be in the fight against climate change?
The swan sanctuary wetland fighting climate change
In November 1946, a naturalist called Peter Scott came to a wild marshy area on the banks of the River Severn, near Slimbridge. He was drawn by the thousands of migrating geese and swans that flew thousands of miles from the Russian Arctic to spend the winter here on the mudflats and marshes.
Captivated, Scott settled in a small cottage and later built a house right on a lake, with a huge window to watch the wildfowl.
He dug lakes and connecting channels, built hides and even towers to watch the birds without disturbing them.
Over the years, the reserve grew and became home to thousands of ducks, swans , geese as well as the migrating wildfowl.

"He really was a pioneer in conservation," said Chris Moore, a historian of Slimbridge and author of Peter Scott and the Birth of Modern Conservation.
As well as creating a safe haven for endangered species, Scott was a vigorous campaigner for nature.
He led the fight to stop commercial whaling, presented some of the BBC's first natural history programmes called live from Slimbridge, and helped set up WWF, the World Wildlife Fund.

items.title: Humans May Have Been Getting High on Weed 2,800 Years Ago. Cannabis Seeds and Hair With Traces of THC Were Found in an Ancient Tomb
items.desc: A tomb discovered in Siberia and associated with Scythians—a nomadic, horse-riding people that once roamed the Eurasian steppe—might provide the earliest direct evidence of cannabis use
items.text:
Cannabis is one of the world’s most widely used psychoactive plants, with millions of people inhaling and ingesting it for its mind-­altering effects. But new research suggests our current relationship with weed is nothing new.
A study published November 5 in the journal Science suggests humans have been getting high on weed for at least 2,800 years—centuries longer than previously thought. The findings seem to offer the earliest direct evidence of cannabis use.
Researchers have long been interested in how ancient people used cannabis. Yet studying it has proven tricky because plants are rarely preserved over long periods of time. Since cannabis has many uses, including the production of oil and fiber, it’s even more challenging to determine whether and when individuals were using it specifically to get high.
In 2017, archaeologists digging in southern Siberia discovered a huge 2,800-year-old tomb that contained the remains of several high-status individuals . The site, called Tunnug 1, is associated with the Scythians , a nomadic, horse-riding culture that occupied the Eurasian steppe from the ninth to the third century B.C.E.
Excavations turned up numerous artifacts, from weapons and animal statues to pieces of gold jewelry and horse gear. But the researchers also found nearly 1,500 whole or partial cannabis seeds at the site, as well as preserved human hair, which allowed them to explore whether the Scythians might have been getting high.
“It’s only so often as an archaeologist that you get to drug test a person that’s been dead for nearly 3,000 years,” lead author Gino Caspari , an archaeologist at the University of Bern in Switzerland and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Germany, tells the New York Times ’ Annie Roth.
Radiocarbon dating traced the seeds to the early eighth century B.C.E., around the same time the burial site is believed to have been constructed. The hair, meanwhile, tested positive for pot. Specifically, the strands contained cannabinol (CBN), a byproduct of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary psychoactive compound in the plant. It also contained weaker chemical signatures consistent with THC.
Caspari tells the Associated Press ’ Jamey Keaten and Philipp Jenne that it’s “extremely rare” for archaeologists to find “both preserved plant parts and human soft tissue with the active compounds in it in the same context.”

items.text:
A woman has had her faith in humanity restored after neighbors arrived on paddleboards to rescue her and her son during recent flooding in Florida.
Emergency services were unable to reach her, the 911 operator said, as Brittany Grant and her son sat on their kitchen counter while floodwaters rose higher and higher above their floor.
Brevard County was recently hit by what weather reports say is a 1,000 year rain event, which flooded towns like Melbourne, Port Lucie, and Palm Bay where Grant lives with her son and 3 dogs.
Having had no luck with 911, Grant turned to Facebook asking for help. Seeing the social media SOS, neighbor Stephanie Fanguy marshalled her strapping teenage sons Jonah, 15, and Lucas, 17, who immediately planned a navigational rescue.
Embarking on an inflatable paddleboard and a borrowed kayak, Jonah and Lucas reached Grant’s house and got to work getting her son Nikoa out through what appeared on social media to be the kitchen window.
Lucas tried to calm Nikoa, who told Click Orlando he struggles with anxiety, by asking him simple questions and remarking humorously at the weather.
Eventually, mother, son, and their 3 dogs—including one which took up half the paddleboard—were all brought to safety.
“The community came together and saved us,” she said . “If it wasn’t for them, I don’t know how we would have gotten out.”
“My faith in humanity has been restored,” she added, saying that other neighbors had volunteered to help as well.
Lucas and Jonah, meanwhile, had a hero’s mentality: someone needed help and they didn’t think twice.

“He just walked right out of the bushes onto a horse trail.” That’s how one rescuer in Kentucky described the moment he spotted 6-year-old Roman Heilman, a boy with autism missing for 3 days.
Jacob Mullins, a member of a local horse trailriding group, told the Lexington Herald Leader that he was only about a half-mile from Heilman’s home when he suddenly climbed out of a bush followed by a small dog, and and sang “Old McDonald.”
Heilman then grabbed onto the leg of the lead rescuer and didn’t want to let go.
He had been reported missing in the late afternoon on Sunday, November 1st, and the volunteers had been out since first light on Tuesday, looking around the wooded and mountainous area for hours, covering some 14 miles.
1 of 10 members of a horse trailriding group who live either side of the Kentucky-West Virginia state line, Jacob Mullins told the Lexington Herald Leader about the moment that the hunters became the hunted.
“We found him probably about a mile and a half from his house. He came out of the bushes saying ‘E-I-E-I-O horsey.’ He just walked right out of the bushes onto a horse trail,” Mullins remembered.
“He was naked, and he was scratched, and he had a little dog with him. He ate a banana and drank some water and then we brought him off the hill.”
Roman is autistic, and when it was reported to police that he had wandered away from his house into the woods, “hundreds” volunteered to aid in the search. This included other teams on horseback, drones, but also motor vehicles, which Mullins thought perhaps had scared the boy from being found earlier.
Rescue authorities had received information on Sunday that the child had removed his clothing at some point, making the situation even more concerning. Indeed, he would have spent two frigid nights in the woods.
Travis Hughes, Director of Lawrence County Emergency Management, put out a heartfelt statement following the rescue on Facebook, in which he said he had “never been more proud” of the community.

“What happened over the course of this search was nothing short of a miracle, and I praise God for that,” said Hughes. “It was also an incredible, overwhelming effort from so many people who came together with one common goal.”

Komtek I by Michael Fossick, who studied at Bradford School of Art, was created in 1962 to celebrate a Hong Kong company that produced microcomputers in the early days of space travel.

Islanders Celebrate Protections of Their Magical Maerl Beds
Fish Stocks Thrive Thanks to This Strange Seaweed and Locals Who Protected It
A ban on industrial scallop dredging has been “the most amazing thing to happen” to the residents, both man and marine, of the Summer Isles.
In place for 10 years, the ban has protected this extraordinary kind of magenta-colored seaweed called maerl, which forms hard, chalky nodules like coral on the seabed, and has allowed for whales, dolphins, porpoises, and key fish stocks to thrive.
Scallop dredging around the Summer Isles had damaged this incredible marine seascape for decades until a coalition of citizen scientists and activists got the activity banned inside a 150,000-acre protected area off the northwest coast of Scotland that contains all the area’s maerl beds, including 2 that are over a mile long which have been growing in the same place for 9,000 years.
Maerl builds up overtime into beds and carpets that interlock, creating magnificent marine habitat for fish species to breed.
Looking somewhat like the pieces from a game of knucklebones, the free movement of water between each nodule provides for excellent circulation which the foundational species of the marine food web need. They in turn provide for the species above and beyond them, all the way up to dolphins and humans.
The protections have been the “most amazing thing to happen to the Summer Isles,” one local activist and artist named Diyanna Ross told the Guardian. “It is an archipelago that is made in heaven for breeding fish.”
The Blue Hope Alliance, of which Ross is a part, also includes an association of Scottish “creel” fishermen, a smaller, more sustainable method of harvesting seafood that doesn’t deplete underlying stocks.
Decades of dredging had severely depleted scallop numbers, requiring industrial fishing operations to damage more and more seabed in search of the bivalves.
The 10-year-old campaign to ban scallop dredging, the Guardian reports , was as much about allowing these creel fishermen to continue to harvest scallops as it was about allowing the scallop to recover.

“It was like looking for a needle in a haystack.”
That’s how Professor Daniel Mège described the discovery of trace volcanic gases on Mars that could be key to finding life on the Red Planet.
The discovery centers around hydrogen chloride gas seeping out through volcanic rifts—something of a “smoking gun” that suggests Mars is not geologically dead, but merely sleeping.
These gases hint at magma, which, when coming into contact with groundwater can produce warm habitable niches for organisms beneath the Red Planet’s surface.
“If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface,” one of the scientists behind the discovery hypothesized.
Mars is studded with the largest volcanoes in the solar system, and fresh fissures on the surface of one of the largest, called Alba Mons, hint at volcanically active spots under the surface.
Detected by a European Space Agency (ESA) orbiter, an international research team believes that the release of hydrogen chloride from these fissures comes from hot magma beneath the surface.
The ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) first reported hydrogen chloride gas in the Martian atmosphere in 2021. The gas is commonly found escaping from magmatic vents on Earth, leading researchers to wonder whether the same was happening on Mars.
Evidence for active volcanism on Mars has always been extremely elusive, yet enough has been identified in the form of geologically-recent lava flows and “marsquakes” over the last 50 years, so as never to rule it out.
Now again, researchers noticed spikes of hydrogen chloride where they shouldn’t have been, and during an odd season in the northern hemisphere of Mars.
Study co-leader Professor Daniel Mège, from the Space Research Center of the Polish Academy of Sciences, said the gas varies seasonally on Mars, reaching its maximum in the northern winter, then mostly disappearing in the summer.
But there was one exception to the pattern, always in the same season and at the same place: above volcanic fissures on the flanks of the Alba Mons volcano, in early summer.

items.text:
On June 29, 1952, a state-of-the-art ocean liner, nearly 1,000 feet long, opened up to the public. Some 70,000 people flooded to its berth in New York City to catch a glimpse of the S.S. United States before it hit the Atlantic for its maiden voyage.
Almost immediately, the liner proved worthy of the intense interest. On July 3, 1952, the S.S. United States reached England in a record-breaking three days, 10 hours and 40 minutes , a speed that has yet to be surpassed to this day by any passenger liner. In its 17-year run, the ship would go on to host numerous notables, including Marilyn Monroe , Walt Disney , Salvador Dalí and even the Mona Lisa , after the painting’s one and only trip to the United States.
On Wednesday, more than 70 years after its record-setting maiden voyage, crowds once again came out in droves to see the legendary liner depart on one last journey. This time, the S.S. United States was heading to the bottom of the sea for a new life as an artificial reef and diving destination in the Gulf of Mexico.
Designed by the prolific 20th century naval architect William Francis Gibbs , the ocean liner represented the peak of post-World War II maritime technology. Over 100 feet longer than the Titanic , the United States contained no wood except the ship’s grand pianos , built with fire-resistant mahogany. “She will have more aluminum in her than Mr. Gibbs cares to say, a design feature that will contribute to the dual goal of strength and relative lightness,” George Horne reported for the New York Times in 1951. “There are other metals that are even more secret.” In fact, its construction was kept entirely out of the public eye.
Throughout the 1950s and ‘60s, the liner completed more than 800 journeys across the Atlantic, carrying more than 1 million passengers, including many celebrities and politicians.
Throughout its 17-year tenure, the S.S. United States carried four presidents: Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower, John F. Kennedy and a young Bill Clinton, who took it to study at Oxford University as a Rhodes Scholar in 1968.
With its intricately designed interior featuring patriotic art, amenities including a movie theater and its unparalleled speed, the S.S. United States provided many passengers with lasting memories.

After 100 years, Gretchen Sollo had a major first: a surprise birthday party, thrown by the Lowe’s employees she sees every day.
Following a stroke, Sollo turned to the aisles of Lowe’s for her daily walk and to keep out of the weather in Bradley, Illinois. She’s since walked an estimated 1,500 miles over five years, creating a daily ritual and friendships with staff members that stretched around the store.
Store associates check on her number of laps and even challenge her to races, joining her on her walks around the store. If there’s ever a day Sollo doesn’t show up, staff members notice and worry.
Store manager Joe Jackson gave her the honorary title of “store mom.”
Once Jackson and staff found out Sollo was turning 100 on November 1, 2026, they knew they had to do something special.
When Sollo showed up for her daily laps on October 30, she was joined by Jackson. Jackson guided Sollo over to a decorated aisle where a blue carpet led to an arch of birthday balloons, a cake and a personalized Lowe’s vest for Sollo. The aisle was lined by around 50 associates (some who came on their day off), friends, family and Sollo’s son Hugh.
“I never wanted a birthday party,” Sollo told People in an exclusive interview, adding “Means I missed out on a lot, I guess.”
A woman who spent a century working, raising a family, and staying active finally took a moment to allow others to show how much they cared – they just had to meet her where she already was.

Researchers discover a potential diagnostic breakthrough for a disease often ⁠discovered after it has already spread
A molecular signal in the blood helps identify microscopic changes that precede development of ovarian cancer, researchers have found, ⁠a potential diagnostic breakthrough for a disease often ⁠discovered after it has already spread.
For decades, ​efforts to detect ovarian cancer earlier have focused on finding smaller tumors, the researchers noted in their report published on Tuesday in Nature Medicine.
“We asked a fundamentally different question: What if we could identify the earliest molecular warning signs before invasive cancer even develops?” study leader Rajan Gogna of the Hoag Family Cancer Institute in ⁠Newport Beach, California, said in a statement.
Ovarian cancer often begins with microscopic changes in the lining of the fallopian tubes. The precancerous lesions are known as serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma.
The new study found that women with this precursor condition have elevated blood levels of an RNA molecule called Tu-Stroma.
When researchers measured Tu-Stroma in blood, they detected STIC in 92.3% of affected women ⁠and correctly identified 98.2% of healthy women.
In women with genetic risk factors for ovarian cancer, approximately 72% of positive results would be accurate, while negative results would be correct nearly 100% of the time, they reported.
“For women at high risk, this ​could transform how we approach prevention,” co-author Dr Esha Madan, also of Hoag, said in a statement.
Many such women ‌face difficult decisions about preventive surgery to remove their fallopian tubes ‌and ovaries.
“Today, decisions about preventive surgery are largely guided by inherited risk, without knowing whether precancerous lesions are actually present,” Madan said. “Our discovery could eventually provide that missing biological information.”

The Maya used so much of this prized pigment that they polluted some of their cities. Now, new research suggests the Maya’s cinnabar-derived mercury contamination was even more widespread than previously thought—and it could have contributed to the civilization’s downfall.

The findings, published November 4 in the journal Science Advances , suggest mercury pollution took a toll on the lakes’ aquatic ecosystems, causing their populations of aquatic creatures to decline or collapse. If the Maya ate fish or drank water from the lakes, they could have been exposed to toxic concentrations of mercury for decades or even centuries.

Japanese artist Yoshitomo Nara is bringing his instantly recognizable characters back to New York with a major exhibition at David Zwirner. Spanning two of the gallery’s Chelsea locations, the presentation features nearly 100 works, including new paintings, drawings, recent sculptures, and selections from earlier decades. It marks Nara’s first solo exhibition with David Zwirner and his first major solo presentation in New York in nearly a decade.
Best known for his oversized, wide-eyed figures, Nara has developed a visual language that balances playful imagery with a rebellious edge. His young-looking subjects often appear innocent at first glance, but their expressions suggest something more complicated. Some stare directly at the viewer with quiet defiance, while others carry an unmistakable sense of melancholy. Beneath their cartoonlike appearance, Nara’s characters confront ideas about childhood, vulnerability, resistance, and the realities of the world around them.
The exhibition also traces the development of Nara’s distinctive style. Earlier works from the late 1980s and 1990s appear alongside new pieces, offering a closer look at how his imagery has evolved. His latest paintings introduce muted colors and layered surfaces, while large-scale monochromatic drawings made with industrial paint sticks reveal the expressive energy of his drawing practice.
At the gallery’s 19th Street location, 13 monumental bronze sculptures transform the space. Coated in matte white, the oversized heads recall the snow-covered forests near Mount Hakkōda in northern Japan, where Nara grew up. Their imposing scale contrasts with their softly illuminated surfaces, creating an atmosphere of stillness. Together, the sculptures connect his familiar characters to the natural landscapes and childhood memories that continue to inform his work.
Yoshitomo Nara is on view at David Zwirner’s galleries at 533 West 19th Street and 537 West 20th Street in New York City from November 5 through December 12, 2026. Visit David Zwirner for additional information and exhibition details.

Levels of the two most toxic "forever" chemicals in England's rivers have dropped by nearly a third over the last decade, according to new figures from the Environment Agency (EA).
The decline in the chemicals, PFOS and PFOA, has been put down to stricter restrictions on their use in products after increasing evidence emerged of their damaging impact on human health and the environment.
One expert studying the impact of the chemicals said it was "brilliant" to see how far the UK has come on this issue.
Thousands of other forever chemicals, known officially as PFAS, remain in use but the regulator said its report showed the need for them all to be better monitored and regulated.
PFAS were first developed in the 1930s in the US and became popular with companies making products like frying pans and firefighting foam because of their useful, oil-resistant, water-resistant and electrical properties.
They are called forever chemicals because their natural resistance means they take a very long time to break down naturally.
The earliest types of these chemicals were called PFOS and PFOA. But two decades ago researchers started to find that they were linked to tissue damage in animals and increased rates of certain serious health conditions such as testicular cancer. , external
As a result, PFOS was all but banned in the UK in 2010 and PFOA in 2020.
The latest data from the regulator, published on Thursday, shows that the concentrations in English rivers of PFOS and PFOA over the last 10 years have now fallen by 30% and 29% respectively.
Levels in freshwater fish have fallen 49%.
"It's brilliant to see how far we have come in the last 10 years," said Dr David Megson, reader in environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University.
There are thought to be around 15,000 other PFAS, although only around 200 are frequently used.
The EA said that despite increasing research into these compounds, "uncertainty remains regarding the toxicity of many PFAS". It said its findings "reinforces the need" for regulating all PFAS rather than one by one.
The chemicals industry has long opposed such an approach, arguing that there is currently no, or limited, evidence to suggest that other PFAS are toxic and that some have vital uses such as in life-saving medical equipment.

items.desc: Most dengue infections cause mild flu-like symptoms or no symptoms at all. But at least one person has died from this year’s outbreak in Florida, where health experts worry the disease will become more common in the future
items.text:
McKenzie Prillaman | Assistant Digital Editor, Science & Innovation
This year, the Florida Department of Health has recorded a staggering 524 locally acquired cases of dengue , a mosquito-borne viral disease, as of October 31. That’s the highest number recorded there since the disease returned to the state in 2009 , according to Forbes ’ John Drake. For context, only 62 locally acquired cases were documented in 2025.
Most infected people either do not show symptoms or experience only mild illness . But in early September, a Tampa-area woman named Gay Rabb Small died of dengue on her 80th birthday, after developing a tremor and going to the emergency room, per the New York Times ’ Anemona Hartocollis.
Later that month, three counties in Florida declared local emergencies over the illness, and in October, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a national emergency response to dengue.
“It is very unusual to have transmission in the United States,” Eva Harris , an infectious diseases expert at the University of California, Berkeley, tells the Times . “This is so very much of an eye-opener.”
Dengue is a viral disease spread by mosquitoes, mainly the species Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus , which are both present in Florida , among other places. The disease is more common in tropical and subtropical regions , where these biting insects thrive, than in temperate climates.
Around three in four infected people are asymptomatic or have mild flu-like symptoms, such as fever, headache, nausea and rash. Muscle and joint pain is another common symptom, which is why the disease is sometimes called “breakbone fever.” Symptoms usually appear within two weeks of being bitten by an infected mosquito and clear up after a week or two.
However, one in four dengue cases becomes severe. Those symptoms include extreme abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, rapid breathing and blood in vomit or stool, and anyone experiencing them should seek medical care. These signs often appear after the fever goes away, and people who have previously been infected are at a greater risk of severe dengue.
Individuals who recover from dengue can continue feeling fatigued for several weeks.
Although dengue vaccines exist , none are currently approved for use in the United States. They’re authorized in nations where the disease is more common, such as Argentina, Brazil, Indonesia and Thailand.

46 years ago today, NASA’s Voyager 1 probe arrived at Saturn and beamed back the first images ever taken of its rings. It arrived at our solar system’s second-largest planet via a gravitational assist trajectory at Jupiter which was replicated with Voyager 2. On November 12th, when the space probe came within 77,000 miles of Saturn’s cloud-tops, the space probe’s cameras detected complex structures in the rings of Saturn, and its remote sensing instruments studied the atmospheres of Saturn and its giant moon Titan. READ what it discovered… (1980)
Voyager 1 found that about 7% of the volume of Saturn’s upper atmosphere is helium (compared with 11% of Jupiter’s atmosphere), while almost all the rest is hydrogen. Since Saturn’s internal helium abundance was expected to be the same as Jupiter’s and the Sun’s, the lower abundance of helium in the upper atmosphere may imply that the heavier helium may be slowly sinking through Saturn’s hydrogen; that might explain the excess heat that Saturn radiates over energy it receives from the Sun.
Winds blow at high speeds on Saturn. Near the equator, the Voyagers measured winds about 500 m/s (1,100 mph). The wind blows mostly in an easterly direction. Voyager measured the rotation of Saturn (the length of a day) at 10 hours, 39 minutes, 24 seconds, and identified polar aurorae, and aurora-like ultraviolet emissions at middle latitudes. These remain a puzzle to this day, since bombardment by electrons and ions, known to cause auroras on Earth, occurs only at the high latitudes.

Photo: Vincent van Gogh via Wikimedia Commons (Public domain)
Despite painting himself around 35 times, there is only one confirmed photographic portrait of Vincent van Gogh that clearly shows his face. Taken in 1873, when the artist was 19 years old, the photograph captures a young Van Gogh staring unsmilingly into the camera, as was common for portrait photography at the time.
Around the time the photograph was taken, Van Gogh was working in the art trade. It would still be several years before he decided to become an artist and began creating the paintings he is known for today.
Photo: Jacobus Marinus Wilhelmus de Louw via Wikimedia Commons (Public domain)
Over the years, several other photographs have been associated with Van Gogh, although most have never been authenticated. One image was believed for decades to show a 13-year-old Vincent. In 2018, however, researchers determined that the boy was actually his younger brother, Theo van Gogh, who was photographed in Brussels at age 15 in 1873.
Photo: Ernest Ladrey via Wikimedia Commons (Public domain)
The mistake is understandable. The brothers shared similar features, and the photograph had been accepted as an image of Vincent for more than 60 years. Once it was correctly identified, the 1873 portrait of 19-year-old Vincent once again became his only known photographic portrait.

Sometimes referred to as a photograph of “Brussels clergymen,” the image has never been authenticated as a portrait of the artist. The Canadian photographer’s information printed on the photograph also makes the identification unlikely, since Van Gogh never traveled outside Europe.

China Switches On World’s Biggest Example of New, Cheap Green Energy Storage
(I think for SEO sake, we could consider keeping the clunkier ‘Liquid Air Energy Storage’ in the headline)
The world’s largest demonstration plant for a new kind of renewable energy storage is up and running in the west of the China.
Called liquid-air energy storage (LAES) the plant uses renewable electricity to compress air to extreme densities until it turns to liquid. It can then be rapidly released to power a turbine and discharge that green energy back into the grid.
China has received numerous plaudits for its rapid adoption of renewable energy at both scale and speed, and this new facility in Qinghai Province brings in a key missing element to the renewable build-out: grid-scale battery storage for when the Sun isn’t shining and the wind isn’t blowing.
Not that either of those happen very often in Qinghai, which encompasses parts of the Tibetan Plateau, and Mongolia-like grasslands and desert, where both sun and wind are famously relentless.
Described as “the world’s largest grid-connected liquid-air energy storage facility by both rated power and energy capacity,” the facility is rated at 600 megawatt-hours, and will substantially back up the renewable contribution to the regional power grid by providing 10 hours of continual power supply when necessary. Additionally, it was built with its own solar farm, rated at 250MW.
LAES works by turning ordinary air into a liquid, keeping that liquid in insulated tanks, and then converting it back into electricity when needed.
When electricity is plentiful, it powers machinery that draws in air, compresses it and cools it to extremely low temperatures of around -190°C. At this point, the air becomes a liquid, taking up far less space than it did as a gas.
When power is needed, the liquid air is pumped to high pressure and warmed. As it warms, it rapidly expands back into a gas and can be used to spin a turbine connected to an electricity generator, sending power back to the grid.
A cool party trick is how the system utilizes the excess heat and cold: it stores both for heating and cooling the air as needed, reducing energy consumption and environmental disturbance.

The gold rush into GLP-1 weight-loss drugs risks diverting pharmaceutical firms’ attention away from diabetes treatments such as insulin, the head of the Access to Medicine Foundation has warned.
GLP-1 blockbuster medications such as Novo Nordisk’s Ozempic and Eli Lilly’s Mounjaro have revolutionised obesity and diabetes treatment but there has been a greater focus by companies on weight loss, according to a report from the Netherlands-based non-profit group.
The group warned that many people cannot even get hold of basic insulin, critical for people with type 1 diabetes, and many countries were struggling to access GLP-1 medications at all – as the explosion in their popularity continues since the weight-loss jab Wegovy launched in 2021.
Diabetes affects an estimated 589 million adults globally, 81% of whom live in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) such as Pakistan, Egypt and Jordan.
“A lot of the GLP-1 drugs are just starting to enter these LMIC markets for obesity,” said Jay Iyer, the foundation’s chief executive, adding: “You have a lot of attention on GLP-1s, but a lot of it is directed towards the obesity market, and that’s not going to help people with type 1 diabetes who after 105 years of insulin development still do not have access to the drug.”
Companies are able to charge far higher prices and enjoy greater profit margins on weight-loss injections and pills , compared with other medication such as insulin.
“There is a risk that any of the three – Sanofi, [Eli] Lilly or Novo [Nordisk]– could leave the insulin market, and that will be disastrous for supply to insulin especially for people living with type 1 diabetes and insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes,” Iyer said.
Denmark’s Novo Nordisk has announced plans to phase out some of its older diabetes products, including insulin pens. However, Sanofi has just broken ground on a new insulin production site at its BioCampus in Frankfurt. The French company supplies insulin to 15 million people in more than 100 countries each year. items.text:
Carlyn Kranking | Associate Web Editor, Science
Matthew Holman , a senior astrophysicist at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, was sifting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile when something odd caught his eye. Running a custom-made computer program, he and his colleague Kevin Napier had already spotted more than 2,000 little bright dots in the telescope data, corresponding to newly discovered small objects in the distant solar system. But this one was different: It seemed to be big.
Holman managed his expectations. After all, astronomers in the business of finding distant objects are used to disappointment. “We all have ‘found Mars’ … in terms of a false positive,” Holman tells Smithsonian magazine. They find a bright object that seems really big, then, with a closer look, learn that it’s nothing very remarkable after all. “We’re all really cautious when you see something that looks like it’s large.”
Still, this object grabbed Holman’s attention, so he tried to verify it with Napier and Rubin solar system lead scientist Mario Jurić . They found the celestial body in previous photos of the sky throughout the past decade, which helped them zero in on its orbital path—and the more historical data they found, the more confident they became.
“We know that it’s real,” Holman says. “Every time you look at the predicted location, there it is.” They even found it in photographic plates from 1937, stored in the Harvard plate stacks , he says.
The object, called 2026 ED138 , is 46 times farther from the sun than Earth is, and it takes 281.1 years to complete an orbit. Now, the central question is whether it’s big enough to be classified as a new dwarf planet, which would put it among the rare ranks of only five other objects in our solar system.
“This is incredibly exciting,” Paul Byrne , a planetary scientist at the Washington University in St. Louis who was not involved in the discovery, tells National Geographic ’s Robin George Andrews. “It heralds a new era of solar system and planetary science.”
Dwarf planets are smaller planets that orbit a star and have a nearly round shape, which happens naturally with objects above a certain size, as their gravitational force pulls evenly on all sides . A viral moment from a doorbell camera that reached millions of people has now raised more than $76,000 to support a woman who spends her days caring for others.
When Suzanna Metcalf arrived at Pastor Neal Seiwert’s home in Castle Rock, Colorado last year, she apologized as she had mixed up their pizza order, and would have to return with the correct order. She blamed “getting old,” but the struggle on her face was clear.
Metcalf works delivery shifts while serving as the full-time caregiver for her 82-year-old mother, managing daily care, medical needs and household expenses.
Instead of frustration, Seiwert, his wife Hailee, and their three young daughters stepped outside, placed their hands on her shoulders, and prayed for her. The short clip, captured by a doorbell camera, showed Metcalf visibly moved by the unexpected kindness after a long day of work.
The video, posted by Seiwert, quickly went viral, with hundreds of commenters, who almost all had the same question: How can we help?
The Seiwerts found Metcalf, and with her permission, started a GoFundMe, which describes Suzanna as a woman who has spent years putting others first.
What began as a modest effort quickly grew. More than 2,600 donors have contributed over the last year, raising over $76,000 — far exceeding the initial $10,000 goal— to give Suzanna some financial breathing room as she continues caring for her mom.
Seiwert told the New York Post he wanted Metcalf to feel both his family’s support and a broader sense of being valued. “So many people are commenting on how it brought them to tears. There are many people who simply just need love,” he said.
A viral moment doesn’t change the demands of caregiving and delivery work. But it has shown, in concrete form, that one small pause for kindness can open the door for real help.

items.title: This Mysterious Combination Lock Sank in a 1583 Shipwreck. When Engineers Cracked the Code, It Clicked Open for the First Time in More Than 400 Years
items.desc: A metal detectorist recovered the brass artifact from the wreck of the "Ann Francis," a merchant vessel that sank off southern Wales. Researchers used micro-CT scans to identify the four-letter combination
items.text:
Ellen Wexler | Writer and Special Projects Editor
In 1999, Peter Hughes stumbled upon the brass combination lock on Margam Beach in Wales. It featured four rotating dials, each bearing six letters. The dials turned smoothly, but only one of 1,296 possible combinations would open the device.
The lock was an artifact from the Ann Francis , a merchant ship that sank in 1583. Hundreds of the vessel’s treasures—including compasses, coins and cannonballs—have since surfaced on the beach. But Hughes was particularly intrigued by the lock. He fiddled with the dials for two decades, trying to solve the puzzle.
Now, researchers have used CT scans to reveal the four-letter code: ANCE. When they tested it out, the lock clicked open for the first time in more than four centuries. “For me, it’s like opening the Ark of the Covenant,” Hughes tells BBC Wales ’ Meleri Williams. “I’m delighted—truly thrilled.”
The Ann Francis was traveling from Spain to England when a storm swept in on December 28, 1583. The winds blew it off course, and it ultimately wrecked off Margam Beach in southern Wales. According to a parish register, 14 sailors died in December 1583, and these men may have been the Ann Francis ’ crew. The record blamed the incident on “the detestable working of an execrable witch.”
As word spread, looters descended upon the beach, prompting legal disputes over the rights to the ship’s treasures. A few months after the wreck, Francis Shaxton, the owner of the Ann Francis , claimed the vessel and recovered some of the items.
For centuries, many more artifacts remained buried beneath the sand. Hughes, a metal detectorist, made his discoveries between 1996 and 2017, aided by dredging and storms that shifted the beach’s sand. He found the combination lock near coin weights and Spanish silver coins—perhaps items that the lock once protected.
“It’s in fantastic condition. It still has its working parts. All of the letters are really clear,” Siân Iles , a senior curator at Museum Wales , says in a video . “I think it’s human nature when you have a code to crack—that’s what you want to do.”
Museum Wales recently acquired Hughes’ trove of artifacts, including the lock. Curators decided to ask researchers at Cardiff University for help identifying the combination.
